Refrigeration control itself is unaffected; the controller is only passing the message along

Voltage jumper settings or a blown board fuse, per KE2's list

causes: The room air probe failed open or shorted
A probe or wire damaged, wet, or iced over inside the box
A transient fault — the alarm clears itself seconds after the probe reads normally again
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||P1.fixable: Partially. The controller has already protected the box by cycling the compressor on a timer, so cooling continues. Staff can verify box temperature with a separate thermometer, look for obvious probe damage, and power-cycle once.
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||P1.why_tech: The manual specifically says check the probe connections before replacing the probe — meter work at the controller terminals. Timed fallback cycling holds the box roughly, not precisely, so don't leave it that way for weeks.

causes: The evaporator coil probe failed, so defrosts now end on time instead of coil temperature
Improperly terminated defrosts letting the coil ice up
A visibly damaged probe wire at the evaporator
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||P2.fixable: No real fix on-site. Staff can check the coil for ice, look for obvious wire damage, and watch box temperature until the probe is replaced — cooling does continue meanwhile.
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||P2.why_tech: Checking connections and replacing the evaporator probe is technician work, and it gets urgent the moment ice starts building on the coil, because an iced coil eventually stops cooling the box.

causes: The optional third probe — often used for condenser temperature monitoring — failed
Refrigeration outputs unchanged; the box should still be cooling normally
Auto-clears when the probe reads normally again
XR-series (XR60CX)||P3.fixable: Nothing needs fixing today: cooling is unaffected. Verify box temperature with a separate thermometer and report the code to your service company.
XR-series (XR60CX)||P3.why_tech: The probe connection needs checking and the probe replacing at the next service visit — while it's out, the controller has lost its condenser high-temperature protection (HA2), which is worth restoring before summer.

causes: The optional fourth probe (connected via the Hot Key plug) failed
Outputs unchanged, cooling continues, and the alarm auto-clears if the probe recovers
XR-series (XR60CX)||P4.fixable: Nothing urgent — cooling continues normally. Verify box temperature with a separate thermometer and log the code.
XR-series (XR60CX)||P4.why_tech: A technician checks the Hot Key probe connection and replaces the probe at the next scheduled visit; this is a monitoring loss, not a refrigeration fault.

causes: Door not fully closed or gasket not sealing
Ice on the evaporator coil or fans not moving air
Condensing unit off, tripped breaker, or a dirty condenser coil with blocked airflow
Warm product loaded before the box recovered
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||HA.fixable: Often. The unit keeps trying to cool (outputs are unchanged) and the alarm silences itself once temperature recovers — so working the door/coil/condenser checklist is genuinely the fix in most cases.
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||HA.why_tech: If temperature isn't dropping within an hour of closing the door and clearing airflow, what remains is refrigerant-side — low charge, a failing compressor — which is gauge work requiring EPA Section 608 certification, with product warming as you wait.

causes: Setpoint recently changed lower than intended
A stuck contactor or control problem keeping the compressor running past setpoint
Freeze-sensitive product parked in the evaporator discharge air
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||LA.fixable: Partially. Verify actual temperature with a separate thermometer, check the setpoint, and move freeze-sensitive product away from the discharge air. The alarm clears itself when temperature normalizes.
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||LA.why_tech: A box that keeps running colder than setpoint points at a stuck contactor or control fault — live electrical diagnosis. In a cooler, every extra hour of overcooling is frozen, ruined product.

causes: Dirty condenser coil — dust, lint, or kitchen grease insulating it
Stored boxes or debris blocking airflow around the condensing unit
A failed condenser fan
Refrigerant-side problems driving head pressure up — the non-DIY tail of the list
XR-series (XR60CX)||HA2.fixable: Frequently, yes — this is the most staff-fixable alarm on the controller. With the disconnect off, brush or vacuum the coil (never pressure-wash into the fins), clear the stored junk, and confirm the fan spins. Note the compressor may have been switched off to protect itself.
XR-series (XR60CX)||HA2.why_tech: If HA2 returns after a genuinely clean coil and free airflow, high head pressure is coming from the refrigerant side — overcharge, non-condensables — and that diagnosis takes gauges and EPA Section 608 certification.

causes: Very low ambient temperature at the condensing unit — the usual winter cause
Head-pressure (low-ambient) controls not doing their job
Depending on the bLL parameter, the compressor may be off while the alarm is active
XR-series (XR60CX)||LA2.fixable: Not really. Note the outdoor temperature and whether the unit is still cooling — that's the useful staff contribution.
XR-series (XR60CX)||LA2.why_tech: Low-ambient operation depends on head-pressure controls (fan cycling, flooding valves) that a technician checks with gauges. If the compressor is being held off in cold weather, the box can still drift warm — don't ignore it because it's winter.

causes: Door open longer than the digital-input delay
A sagging door or damaged gasket/hinges holding the switch open
The plunger or magnetic door switch stuck, iced, or knocked out of alignment
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||dA.fixable: Usually. Close and latch the door, check gasket and hinges, and free or realign a stuck or iced switch — the alarm stops the moment the switch closes. Note the compressor and fans may have been paused while the door read open.
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||dA.why_tech: If dA stays on with the door verifiably closed, the switch or its wiring has failed and needs testing and replacement — a quick technician visit, but meter work all the same.

causes: Whatever device the installer wired to the digital input has tripped — commonly a condensate overflow switch or a high-pressure switch indicator
Refrigeration outputs are unchanged; the controller is only relaying the signal
Clears when the external device resets
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||EA.fixable: Depends entirely on what's wired in, which varies by installer. Staff can check the obvious suspects — condensate overflow, pressure switch indicator — and confirm cooling is still normal.
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||EA.why_tech: If nobody on site can identify or reset the device behind the alarm, a technician has to trace the input wiring. An EA that keeps returning means the external device keeps finding a real problem.

causes: A digital input configured as serious alarm has tripped and the controller switched ALL outputs off
On the XR60CX, the pressure switch alarm reached its set number of trips — that variant only recovers via a power off/on
Blocked condenser airflow or a tripped breaker upstream of the pressure switch
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||CA.fixable: No — and it's urgent, because refrigeration is stopped. Staff can check for obvious condenser blockage or a tripped breaker and move product if help is far off. Do not keep resetting power to force it to run.
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||CA.why_tech: Repeated pressure-switch trips are the system reporting a real refrigeration-side fault; forcing restarts just hammers the compressor. Diagnosis needs gauges and EPA Section 608 certification, and with all outputs off, product loss is on the clock.

causes: The keypad is locked and someone pressed a key — this is a status message, not a fault
The lock exists precisely to stop accidental setpoint changes
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||OF / PoF.fixable: Completely. Hold the UP and DOWN arrows together for more than 3 seconds until the display shows "on" (XR06CX) or "Pon" (XR60CX) — unlocked. Nothing about refrigeration has changed.
XR-series (XR06CX/XR60CX)||OF / PoF.why_tech: The only scenario needing service is a keypad that refuses to unlock after the correct hold, which points to a failed keypad or controller.

causes: The walk-in door left open longer than the Door Al Delay setting
A damaged gasket, closer, or latch — or ice on them — keeping the door from sealing
A door switch failed, stuck, or out of alignment
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.fixable: Usually. Close the door fully, press ALARM to silence the buzzer, and check gasket, closer, latch, and switch alignment — that covers the common cases.
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.why_tech: If the alarm persists with the door genuinely closed, the switch or its wiring needs continuity testing — a short technician task, but meter work on the control circuit.
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.question: Why is my Norlake walk-in showing DOOR AJAR ALARM?

causes: The door left open too long — Norlake flags this as the most common trigger for this early warning
Ice on the evaporator coil or fans not running
Condensing unit off or its coil airflow blocked
A tripped breaker on the refrigeration circuit
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.fixable: Often. Close the door and press ALARM — that silences and deliberately delays the alarm while temperature recovers — then verify coil, fans, condensing unit, and breaker. Most of these resolve without a truck roll.
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.why_tech: If the room doesn't come back to range after the door is closed and airflow verified, the remaining causes are refrigerant-side — sealed-system diagnosis under EPA Section 608 — and warm product doesn't wait.

A stuck cooling relay or contactor keeping refrigeration running past setpoint
Freeze-sensitive product sitting in the evaporator discharge air
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.fixable: Partially. Verify the real temperature with a separate thermometer, check the SET screens for changed setpoints, and move freeze-sensitive product out of the discharge air.
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.why_tech: A room that keeps running below setpoint points at a stuck relay or contactor — live electrical diagnosis in the control panel — and in a cooler, sustained overcooling freezes product.

The controller running on fallback — "USING PROD SENSOR" if the product sensor took over, or "SENSOR FAIL MODE" timed cycling if every sensor is gone
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.fixable: No — but staff should check the MENU 1 status line to see which fallback the controller is in, verify box temperature with a separate thermometer, and record both for the tech. Fallback keeps the room alive, not well-controlled.
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.why_tech: The room is running on backup control, which holds temperature roughly at best — timed cycling can drift either direction. The sensor needs testing and replacement promptly, before backup control turns into a product problem.

A tripped breaker on the evaporator fan circuit
Ice physically blocking the fan blades or coil
A failed blower motor or belt — the alarm screen itself says check blower and belts
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.fixable: Partially. Look at the evaporator — are the blades turning? Check the fan-circuit breaker and look for ice jamming the blades. A tripped breaker or visible ice block is staff-resolvable; a dead motor is not.
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.why_tech: If the fans won't run with power confirmed on, motor, belt, or contactor replacement is a service job. With no air moving across the coil, the room stops cooling regardless of how well the refrigeration side works.

A building outage, or something more local like a failing breaker or wiring issue if it recurs without a known outage
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.fixable: Yes — this one is informational. Press ALARM to view and acknowledge it, confirm room and product temperatures recovered, and check whether other equipment on the circuit also blinked.
Programmable Controller (Carel PCO5+ bas.why_tech: The alarm never affects control of the room. The only reason to bring in an electrician or tech is repeated power interruptions with no known outage — that pattern points at a failing breaker or wiring fault worth catching early.

causes: The Sair air temperature sensor has failed outright
The sensor's electrical connection is lost — a damaged, iced-over, or dangling probe near the evaporator return air
A wiring break between the probe and the controller
ERC 211/213/214||E29.fixable: Partly. Staff can power-cycle the unit at the breaker for a few minutes and check the probe for visible damage or ice — sometimes a glitch clears. If E29 comes back, it isn't a staff fix.
ERC 211/213/214||E29.why_tech: Testing the sensor circuit means live electrical measurement at the controller terminals, and while the alarm is active the box is running blind on air temperature — every hour of guessing puts product at risk.

causes: The S5 evaporator (defrost) sensor is defective
Its electrical connection to the controller is lost
With the sensor out, defrost runs on time only, so the evaporator can ice up — heavy ice on the coil is the visible symptom
ERC 211/213/214||E27.fixable: Only the first steps. A power cycle at the breaker occasionally clears a glitch, and staff can keep the door shut and watch box temperature. A sensor that stays failed is a service part.
ERC 211/213/214||E27.why_tech: Replacing and verifying the S5 sensor is live electrical work at the controller, and an unmanaged icing coil will eventually choke airflow and stop the box from cooling at all.

causes: The Sc condenser sensor is defective
Its electrical connection is lost
While it's down, the controller has no condenser-temperature protection — a dust-matted or blocked condenser could go undetected
ERC 211/213/214||E30.fixable: Staff can power-cycle once and clear any obvious dust or cardboard away from the condenser coil, which is worth doing anyway since the unit's own protection is offline. The sensor itself is not a staff repair.
ERC 211/213/214||E30.why_tech: The sensor and its wiring need live electrical testing, and until it's fixed nothing is watching the condenser — a dirty coil that can't reject heat will quietly cook the compressor.

causes: Door left open or a leaking gasket loading the box with warm, humid air
Warm product just loaded, or the door held open for restocking
Heavy ice on the evaporator choking airflow
A dust-matted or blocked condenser that can't reject heat
Condensing unit not running at all — tripped breaker or dead fan
ERC 211/213/214||A01.fixable: Often, yes. Door, gasket, recent loading, blocked condenser airflow, and a tripped breaker are all things staff can find and fix in minutes.
ERC 211/213/214||A01.why_tech: If temperature doesn't recover within an hour of those checks, the fault is in the sealed system or controls — refrigerant diagnosis needs gauges and EPA Section 608 certification, and product is at risk the whole time it stays warm.

causes: Product stacked directly against the air sensor or in the discharge air stream, fooling the reading
The compressor running nonstop instead of cycling off
A sensor or setpoint problem making the controller drive the box too cold
ERC 211/213/214||A02.fixable: Partly. Staff can verify the real temperature with a separate thermometer, move product away from the sensor and discharge air, and pull freeze-sensitive stock out of the cold spots. If the unit won't cycle off, that's it for DIY.
ERC 211/213/214||A02.why_tech: A unit that never cycles off has a controller, sensor, or setpoint fault that takes live electrical testing to pin down — and every hour it runs, produce, dairy, and drinks are freezing.

causes: Supply voltage to the unit is above the safe limit
A building electrical problem on the circuit — the same issue that makes lights flicker or trips other equipment
ERC 211/213/214||A99.fixable: No. Staff can note whether other equipment on the circuit is acting up and watch box temperature, but supply voltage is not something to work around. Don't reset repeatedly — the alarm exists to protect the compressor.
ERC 211/213/214||A99.why_tech: This is building electrical work — live voltage measurement and correction at the panel is electrician territory, and forcing the compressor to run on bad voltage risks destroying it.

causes: Supply voltage sagging below the safe limit
The unit sharing a circuit with heavy equipment that just started
An extension cord or undersized power feed starving the unit
ERC 211/213/214||AA1.fixable: Only the obvious part: if the unit is on an extension cord or a shared circuit with heavy equipment, that's visible and worth flagging. The electrical fix itself is not DIY.
ERC 211/213/214||AA1.why_tech: Sustained low voltage burns out compressor motors — an electrician has to measure the supply under load and correct the feed before the compressor pays the price.

causes: A dust- or lint-matted condenser coil that can't reject heat
Boxes, bags, or debris blocking airflow through or around the coil
A condenser fan that has stopped running
ERC 211/213/214||A61.fixable: Usually, yes — this is the classic staff-fixable alarm. Kill power at the breaker, brush or vacuum the coil face, clear everything blocking airflow, confirm the fan spins, and see if the alarm clears as the unit cools.
ERC 211/213/214||A61.why_tech: If the coil is clean and airflow is clear but A61 returns, the fan motor or the refrigerant side is at fault — that's live motor testing and gauge work, and running hot shortens compressor life by the day.

causes: Condenser temperature climbed high enough that the controller locked out — it requires a manual reset (r12 switch off/on or a power-down)
A dirty, dust-matted condenser coil
Blocked airflow around the condensing unit
A condenser fan that isn't spinning
ERC 211/213/214||A80.fixable: Once. Clean the coil and clear the airflow first, then reset by powering down at the breaker for a few minutes. Watch it for 30 minutes. If A80 comes back, stop resetting.
ERC 211/213/214||A80.why_tech: Repeated high condenser temperature kills compressors — if one cleaning and one reset don't hold, a tech needs to check the fan motor and pressures before the lockouts turn into a compressor replacement.

causes: The door genuinely open too long — every minute open loads the box with warm, humid air
A torn or iced gasket, or product blocking the door from sealing
A door switch plunger that's stuck or iced up
ERC 211/213/214||A04.fixable: Usually, yes. Shut the door, confirm the latch engages, check the gasket for tears and ice, and free a stuck switch plunger. The alarm should clear within a few minutes of a proper close.
ERC 211/213/214||A04.why_tech: If the alarm stays on with the door verifiably shut, the door switch or its setting is faulty — that's controller wiring and configuration work, and depending on setup the unit may be stopping the compressor and fans every time it thinks the door is open.

causes: An external device wired to the controller's digital input is signaling an alarm
Commonly a pressure switch or other protective device doing its job — what it means depends entirely on what's connected
ERC 211/213/214||A15.fixable: No. Staff can check whether the box is still cooling, note other equipment alarms in the room, and record the code and time — that record genuinely shortens the service call.
ERC 211/213/214||A15.why_tech: Only someone who can trace the installation's wiring can identify which device tripped the input, and if it's a pressure safety, the underlying refrigerant-side problem needs EPA Section 608-certified diagnosis.

causes: Someone switched the unit off at the r12 main switch — a deliberate software on/off, not a fault
An external switch wired to the controller's input put it in standby (cleaning or service, usually)
ERC 211/213/214||A45.fixable: Yes, if it was deliberate — find who turned it off and turn it back on, or flip the external main switch if one is fitted. Don't leave product sitting in a box that's in standby; verify the temperature.
ERC 211/213/214||A45.why_tech: If nobody turned it off and there's no external switch to find, the r12 setting or DI configuration has to be checked in the controller's parameters — a wrong guess there stops cooling entirely.

causes: Door or lid open or not sealing — a torn gasket loads the box with warm, humid air
Warm product just loaded, or a defrost just ended — recovery takes time
Ice on the evaporator or a dirty, blocked condenser
Condensing unit not running — tripped breaker
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A1.fixable: Often, yes. Doors, gaskets, recent loading, post-defrost recovery, condenser blockage, and breakers are all staff checks. Give it up to an hour to pull back down after fixing the obvious.
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A1.why_tech: If temperature doesn't recover within that hour, the problem is in the sealed system or controls — that's gauge work requiring EPA Section 608 certification, and warm product is a countdown clock. Log temperatures for your inspection records while you wait.

causes: Product stacked against the air sensor, fooling the reading
The compressor running continuously and never cycling off
A sensor, relay, or setpoint fault driving the box below the A14 limit
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A2.fixable: Partly. Verify the real temperature with a separate thermometer, clear the sensor, and move freeze-sensitive product away from the discharge air. A unit that won't cycle off is beyond staff.
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A2.why_tech: Diagnosing whether the sensor, relay, or setpoint is at fault means live electrical testing at the controller — and while it runs cold, product in a cooler is freezing.

causes: Door open longer than the alarm delay — open-door time loads the box with warm, humid air
Gasket damage, ice, or product keeping the door off its seal
A sticking or iced door switch
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A4.fixable: Usually, yes. Close and latch the door, check the gasket, free the switch. Depending on setup, refrigeration and fans stop while the controller thinks the door is open — so a stuck switch means no cooling.
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A4.why_tech: If the alarm won't clear with the door shut, the door switch or its wiring is faulty — live testing of the switch circuit and the A04 delay setting is controller work.

causes: Refrigeration stopped deliberately via the r12 main switch
A DI input (an external switch) put the controller in standby — note the AK-CC 210 does not activate its alarm relay for this state, so nothing else may be flagging it
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A45.fixable: Yes, if someone put it in standby for cleaning or stocking — switch it back and verify box temperature. If nobody did, stop guessing at parameters.
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A45.why_tech: Checking the r12 parameter and DI wiring means going into the controller's setup — a wrong change there keeps the box off. Meanwhile a unit in unnoticed standby is warming product with no alarm relay to warn anyone.

causes: Staff activated cleaning mode via the DI input — a deliberate signal, not a fault
The cleaning switch left in the cleaning position after the job was done
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A59.fixable: Yes. Confirm someone actually started a cleaning, return the switch to normal when finished, and verify the case pulls back down to temperature. On networked systems the event is logged as documentation of the cleaning.
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||A59.why_tech: If the unit stays in cleaning mode after the switch is returned to normal, the DI input or its configuration is faulty — controller-level diagnosis, and the case isn't refrigerating properly until it's resolved.

causes: An internal fault in the controller's own electronics — the 'EKC error'
Not a temperature condition: the hardware itself is the problem
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||E1.fixable: One shot: power-cycle at the breaker for a few minutes. If E1 returns, there's nothing else staff can do except record it and watch box temperature with a separate thermometer.
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||E1.why_tech: A persistent internal fault means the controller likely needs replacement — swapping and reprogramming a refrigeration controller is live electrical work, and until then the box's control can't be trusted.

causes: The S5 sensor (defrost/evaporator, or condenser if configured that way) has failed
With it down, defrost control falls back to time-based operation — coil ice-up is the risk, and heavy ice on the evaporator is the visible symptom
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||E27.fixable: Only the checks: look for coil ice, power-cycle once, and monitor box temperature while waiting. The sensor itself is a service part.
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||E27.why_tech: Testing and replacing the S5 sensor is live electrical work at the controller, and an iced coil left unmanaged will eventually block airflow and stop the box from holding temperature.

causes: The Sair air temperature sensor has failed
A damaged or iced probe in the return air stream
A broken connection between probe and controller
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||E29.fixable: Barely. Power-cycle once and inspect the probe for visible damage. If E29 returns, regulation and temperature alarms are unreliable until a tech replaces the sensor — the box is running blind.
EKC 202 / AK-CC 210||E29.why_tech: The sensor circuit needs live electrical testing, and with no trustworthy air reading, neither control nor the alarms protecting your product can be relied on — monitor with a separate thermometer and move product if it drifts.

causes: The S3 air sensor (typically mounted before the evaporator) has failed
A lost connection between the sensor and the controller
Any regulation that uses S3 is unreliable while the fault is active
AK-CC 210/250||E25.fixable: Staff can verify box temperature with a separate thermometer, power-cycle once at the breaker, and record the code and time for the tech. That's the limit.
AK-CC 210/250||E25.why_tech: Confirming whether the sensor or its wiring failed takes live electrical measurement at the controller — and until it's fixed, temperature control on that sensor can't be trusted.

causes: The S4 air sensor (typically mounted after the evaporator) has failed
A lost connection between the sensor and the controller
Regulation and alarm functions using S4 are affected while it's down
AK-CC 210/250||E26.fixable: Same as any failed sensor: verify the real temperature independently, power-cycle once, note the code for the service visit. Replacement is not a staff job.
AK-CC 210/250||E26.why_tech: Sensor and wiring testing is live electrical work, and with S4 out, some of the controller's alarm functions are blind — problems can develop without warning until it's repaired.

causes: An external device wired to the DI2 digital input tripped and held past the configured delay
Often a protective switch that opened for a reason — what it means depends on what the installer wired to DI2
AK-CC 210/250||A16.fixable: No. Check the box is still cooling, note any other alarms on nearby equipment, and record the code and time — that's real help for the tech, not a fix.
AK-CC 210/250||A16.why_tech: Only someone who can trace the installation can identify the device on DI2, and if it's a pressure or safety switch, the root cause behind the trip needs professional diagnosis before the unit is trusted again.

causes: Temperature exceeded the food-safety limit the controller's HACCP function tracks
The same drivers as any high-temperature event: door and gasket leaks letting humid air in, recent loading, evaporator ice, or a dirty condenser that can't reject heat
AK-CC 210/250||A60.fixable: The response is staff work even when the cause isn't: log the actual product and box temperature immediately, check door, loading, coil ice, and condenser airflow, and follow your food-safety procedure for time/temperature abuse — move or discard product per policy.
AK-CC 210/250||A60.why_tech: If temperature doesn't recover quickly, the mechanical cause needs a certified tech, and the event itself must be documented for HACCP records — this alarm is as much a compliance event as an equipment one.

causes: Suction pressure below the safe limit — the controller stops the compressor to protect it
Low refrigerant charge
An iced or starved evaporator — heavy coil ice, dead evaporator fans, or product blocking airflow
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.fixable: Only the airflow part: check the evaporator for heavy ice and confirm the fans run and product isn't blocking them. Do not repeatedly reset the alarm — that short-cycles the compressor.
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.why_tech: Low-pressure trips usually mean a refrigerant or airflow problem that takes gauges and EPA Section 608 certification to diagnose — and with the compressor stopped, product loss is on the clock.

causes: The high-pressure (or combined high/low pressure) safety input tripped and the controller stopped the compressor
Very often a dirty or blocked condenser that can't reject heat
A condenser fan that isn't running
Material stacked around the condensing unit choking its airflow
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.fixable: The most common cause is: with power off at the breaker, brush or vacuum the coil face, clear everything around the unit, confirm the fan runs. Restore power once and monitor — do not keep resetting a pressure trip.
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.why_tech: Repeated high-pressure trips damage the compressor, and forcing restarts against a pressure safety is how condensing units die. If it trips again after a cleaning, the refrigerant side needs certified diagnosis immediately — the box isn't cooling while the compressor is locked out.

causes: Refrigeration stopped via the r12 main switch — deliberate standby, not a fault
The DI1 input (an external switch) stopped the unit; per the manual, r12 and/or DI1 restart regulation
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.fixable: Yes, if someone shut it down on purpose — check with staff, check any external switch wired to DI1, and verify box temperature since the unit hasn't been cooling.
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.why_tech: If nobody stopped it, the r12 setting or DI1 wiring has to be checked inside the controller's configuration — guesswork there keeps the condensing unit off and the box warming.

causes: Airflow through the condenser has dropped — the manual's stated action is to clean the condensing unit
Leaves, lint, dust, or debris matted on the coil
Space around the unit blocked so it can't breathe
A condenser fan not spinning freely
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.fixable: Yes — this is the alarm the manual tells you to fix with a cleaning. Power off at the breaker, remove debris from the coil, clear the space around the unit, check the fan spins freely, restore power, and confirm the alarm clears.
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.why_tech: If A80 comes back after a thorough cleaning, the fan motor or system pressures are at fault — live motor testing and gauge work, and a condenser that can't reject heat is steadily overworking the compressor.

causes: Compressor discharge gas temperature over its limit — the controller steps in to protect the compressor
Blocked or dirty condenser airflow
The unit enclosed in a hot, unventilated space
Refrigerant-side problems driving discharge temperature up
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.fixable: Only the airflow checks: clean visible dirt off the condenser (power off first) and make sure the unit isn't boxed into a hot corner. Avoid repeated resets.
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.why_tech: Overheating discharge gas destroys compressors if the root cause isn't fixed — the refrigerant-side diagnosis behind it is gauge work for an EPA Section 608-certified tech, not something to reset past.

causes: An internal fault in the Optyma Plus controller's own electronics ('Ctrl. Error')
Not an operating condition — the control hardware itself is the problem
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.fixable: One power cycle at the breaker for a few minutes. If E1 returns, record it and watch box temperature — there is no further staff step.
Optyma Plus condensing unit controller||.why_tech: A persistent controller fault means professional testing or replacement of the control board — live electrical work on the condensing unit — and until then the unit's protections and regulation can't be trusted.

causes: The virtual regulation probe the controller regulates on has failed or is returning an invalid reading
An air sensor bulb encased in ice or knocked out of position
A pinched or cut probe cable where it enters the controller
ir33 / ir33+||rE.fixable: Partly. Check whether the displayed temperature is frozen, blank, or wildly wrong, clear ice from the sensor bulb, look over the visible cable, and power-cycle once. If rE returns, stop.
ir33 / ir33+||rE.why_tech: Testing and replacing the probe means live electrical work inside the panel, and while rE is active the controller can't control on real temperature — product is exposed the whole time.

causes: The S1 room (air) probe is faulty, disconnected, or reading out of range
Ice built up around the probe, or the probe knocked loose by product or a pallet
Damaged probe wiring
ir33 / ir33+||E0.fixable: The visual checks are: clear ice from around the probe, make sure it hasn't been hit, inspect the visible wire, power-cycle once. Depending on setup the controller may limp along on timed compressor cycling, but that's a stopgap, not a fix.
ir33 / ir33+||E0.why_tech: A failed room probe means the box is running blind and product is at risk — probe testing and replacement is live electrical work at the controller that shouldn't wait.

causes: The S2 evaporator/defrost probe is faulty or disconnected
Defrosts ending on time instead of coil temperature — leading to iced coils or over-long defrosts
Ice encasing the probe on the coil
ir33 / ir33+||E1.fixable: Staff can spot the symptoms — an iced evaporator coil, defrosts running much longer or shorter than usual — and power-cycle once. Probe replacement is a service job.
ir33 / ir33+||E1.why_tech: The probe has to be tested and replaced at the controller under power, and a coil icing up behind a dead defrost probe will eventually block airflow and take the box down.

causes: An auxiliary probe is faulty or disconnected — S3 (typically the condenser probe) for E2; E3 and E4 are the same fault on probes S4 and S5
Damage to the small sensor wire at the condensing unit
While it's active, condenser-temperature protection may not be working
ir33 / ir33+||E2.fixable: Note which code shows (E2, E3, or E4), look over the sensor wire without opening anything, clear dust from around the condenser since its protection is offline, and power-cycle once. That's the extent of it.
ir33 / ir33+||E2.why_tech: Auxiliary probe testing and replacement is live electrical work, and with the condenser probe out, a dust-matted coil that can't reject heat has nothing watching it.

causes: Door open or gasket not sealing — an open door loads the box with warm, humid air
Warm product just loaded or heavy door traffic during stocking
A defrost that just ended — temperatures run higher right after one
A dust-blocked condenser coil or a condenser fan that isn't running
A tripped breaker on the condensing unit
ir33 / ir33+||HI.fixable: Often, yes — this alarm resets itself once the box pulls back down. Door, gasket, recent loading, post-defrost recovery, condenser airflow, and the breaker are all staff checks.
ir33 / ir33+||HI.why_tech: If temperature keeps climbing or hasn't recovered within an hour or two with the door shut, the fault is mechanical — refrigerant-side diagnosis needs EPA Section 608 certification, and warm product doesn't wait.

causes: A probe drifting cold and triggering a false alarm — verify with an independent thermometer
Product stacked against the air sensor or in the discharge air stream
A compressor that runs nonstop and never cycles off
ir33 / ir33+||LO.fixable: Partly. Confirm the real temperature independently, move product off the sensor, silence the buzzer, and watch whether temperature climbs back — the alarm resets automatically when it recovers.
ir33 / ir33+||LO.why_tech: A box genuinely running colder than setpoint, or a compressor that won't cycle off, is a control or refrigeration fault needing live testing — and in the meantime it's freezing product.

causes: The digital input configured as an immediate external alarm tripped — an external device like a pressure switch or monitoring contact opened
A dirty or blocked condenser tripping an external pressure safety
A condensing unit that's stopped — tripped breaker
ir33 / ir33+||IA.fixable: The side checks are: confirm the condensing unit runs, check its breaker, clear condenser airflow, and log when and how often IA appears. It resets itself when the contact closes — but repeats mean a real problem.
ir33 / ir33+||IA.why_tech: Identifying which safety device tripped requires tracing the installation's wiring, and a pressure safety that keeps opening points to a refrigerant-side fault needing certified diagnosis.

causes: The external alarm contact held open longer than the A7 delay — same trigger as IA, just time-delayed
A condensing unit that isn't running — tripped breaker
Condenser airflow choked by dust, cardboard, or debris, tripping an external safety
ir33 / ir33+||dA.fixable: Same staff scope as IA: verify the condensing unit runs, clear the condenser area, and note whether the alarm lines up with hot weather or heavy door traffic. The device that tripped isn't staff-serviceable.
ir33 / ir33+||dA.why_tech: The external device on the alarm input has to be identified and tested by someone who knows the installation — repeated dA trips mean a protective device keeps finding a reason to open.

causes: The walk-in door genuinely open longer than allowed — every open minute loads the box with warm, humid air
Product, a hose, a pallet, or a strip curtain blocking the door
A torn gasket or ice holding the door off its seal
A dirty, misaligned, or faulty door switch (plunger or magnet)
ir33 / ir33+||dor.fixable: Usually, yes. Close the door properly, clear whatever blocks it, check the gasket, and check the switch clicks when the door shuts — the alarm should clear within a few minutes.
ir33 / ir33+||dor.why_tech: If dor stays on with the door verifiably closed, the door switch or its wiring is faulty — that's live testing at the controller, and control behavior may be altered the whole time the unit thinks the door is open.

causes: The defrost on evaporator 1 hit its maximum time (dP1) before reaching end-defrost temperature — usually heavier-than-normal ice on the coil (Ed2 is the same on evaporator 2)
Humid air infiltration through a leaking door gasket — the most common cause of coil icing
A weak defrost heater, bad defrost probe, or an undersized defrost schedule
Ice or standing water in the drain pan and line
ir33 / ir33+||Ed1.fixable: The detective work is: look at the coil right after the next defrost for leftover ice, check the door gasket and closure, eyeball the drain pan, and note whether Ed1 shows after every defrost or just occasionally.
ir33 / ir33+||Ed1.why_tech: If it repeats, the defrost heater, probe, or schedule needs service — heater testing is live electrical work — and left alone the coil ices solid and the box stops cooling.

causes: Condenser temperature past the pre-alarm level — an early 'dirty condenser' warning while control still runs normally
Dust, lint, cardboard, or grease matting the coil fins so it can't reject heat
Items stored against or on top of the condensing unit blocking its airflow
A hot location — a baking mechanical room or direct sun

ir33 / ir33+||cht.why_tech: If the pre-alarm keeps returning after airflow is cleared, the coil needs a proper professional cleaning and a pressure check — running hot is steadily stressing the compressor.

causes: Condenser temperature over the alarm threshold — the escalated, manual-reset version of the cht warning
A condenser fan that has stopped
A heavily dirt-matted coil or blocked airflow that the earlier warning stage didn't get fixed
ir33 / ir33+||CHt.fixable: The airflow causes are staff-fixable — fan check, clear blockages, spot a filthy coil — but do not repeatedly reset this alarm to keep the box running. It's manual-reset for a reason.
ir33 / ir33+||CHt.why_tech: Prolonged running against a hard high-condenser alarm trips safeties and damages the compressor — a tech needs to clean the coil properly and verify pressures before the unit racks up real damage.

Low refrigerant charge
A heavily iced evaporator coil starving the system and dropping pressure
Evaporator fans not running, or door-gasket infiltration icing the coil

ir33 / ir33+||LP.why_tech: Pressure diagnosis takes gauges and EPA Section 608 certification, and repeated LP trips usually mean a leak or an icing problem — both get worse, not better, while unaddressed.

causes: On pump-down systems, low pressure wasn't reached within the maximum allowed time at shutoff
A liquid-line solenoid valve, pressure switch, or refrigerant-side problem
ir33 / ir33+||Pd.fixable: No. Note when the alarm occurs — every compressor stop, or occasionally — check the breaker, and leave the parameters alone. That's the useful staff contribution.
ir33 / ir33+||Pd.why_tech: Pump-down faults involve the liquid-line solenoid and pressure controls, which need instruments and refrigerant-side access to diagnose — EPA Section 608 territory, not a reset-and-hope situation.

Until it's reset, scheduled time-of-day defrosts and HACCP time-stamping won't run correctly

ir33 / ir33+||Etc.why_tech: A clock that won't hold its setting points to failed clock hardware in the controller — that's a service replacement, and until then defrost scheduling and food-safety time-stamps can't be trusted.

causes: A memory (EEPROM) error in the controller's unit/machine parameters
Stored configuration possibly corrupted — control behavior can't be trusted while this is active

ir33 / ir33+||EE.why_tech: If EE returns, the controller needs reprogramming from a known-good record or outright replacement — and until a tech does that, the box is running on settings that may be corrupt.

causes: A memory error in the controller's operating parameters — setpoints and working values
Stored settings possibly corrupted, same class of fault as EE

ir33 / ir33+||EF.why_tech: The program has to be reloaded from a known-good record by someone who has it — running a walk-in on corrupted setpoints risks both warm product and freeze damage, in either direction.

causes: A HACCP temperature excursion was recorded: HA logs time above the high-temperature threshold in normal operation, HF logs a high-temperature condition after a power failure

ir33 / ir33+||HA.why_tech: Repeated excursions with no obvious cause mean the equipment needs professional diagnosis — and product disposition after an excursion is a call for your food-safety manager, documented for HACCP records.

causes: Temperature at the antifreeze probe fell below its threshold and the manual-reset antifreeze protection tripped
Product or an airflow blockage creating an abnormally cold spot at the sensor
A pattern tied to defrost or nighttime setback timing

ir33 / ir33+||AFr.why_tech: If it repeats, the antifreeze setpoint, probe placement, or system control needs professional review — a protection that keeps tripping is either misconfigured or catching a real freeze risk.

ir33 / ir33+||dEF.why_tech: A display stuck in dEF far beyond normal, or a box that won't recover temperature after defrost, points to a defrost termination or control fault — heater and probe testing is live electrical work.

Ice buildup or physical damage at the air probe
Product buried against the sensor

PJ Easy (PJEZ)||E0.why_tech: The controller can no longer regulate on real air temperature — probe testing and replacement is live electrical work, and the box is effectively blind until it's done.

PJ Easy (PJEZ)||E1.why_tech: Replacing the defrost probe means working in the live control circuit, and a coil that never fully clears will ice over and choke the evaporator until the box can't hold temperature.

Damage to the small sensor wire at the condensing unit
High-condenser-temperature protection is compromised while it's down

PJ Easy (PJEZ)||E2.why_tech: The probe needs live testing and replacement, and until then nothing is watching for a dust-matted condenser that can't reject heat — the exact condition this probe exists to catch.

causes: The digital input configured as an external alarm (parameter A4, delay A7) tripped — an external safety or monitoring contact opened
A stopped condensing unit or tripped breaker
Condenser airflow blockage tripping an external safety
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||IA.fixable: Confirm the condensing unit runs, check the breaker, clear condenser airflow, find out from your installer what's wired to the input, and log occurrences. Diagnosing the device itself isn't DIY.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||IA.why_tech: A repeating external alarm means a protective device keeps finding a reason to open — identifying and testing it takes someone who knows the installation, and if it's a pressure safety, certified refrigerant-side diagnosis.

causes: The door switch reports the door open too long ('dr' on some PJEZ models) — open-door time raises temperature and ices the coil faster with humid air
Something blocking the door, or a torn/iced gasket preventing a seal
A misaligned door switch that doesn't actuate when the door shuts
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||dOR.fixable: Usually, yes. Close the door fully, remove obstructions, inspect the gasket, check the switch alignment, and confirm the alarm clears a few minutes after a proper close.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||dOR.why_tech: If the alarm stays on with the door verifiably closed, the switch or its wiring is at fault — live circuit testing at the controller.

causes: Temperature below the AL threshold longer than the Ad delay — buzzer and relay active until it recovers
A drifting probe giving a false cold reading
Product stacked against the sensor
A compressor that never cycles off

PJ Easy (PJEZ)||LO.why_tech: A unit genuinely running below setpoint continuously has a control or refrigeration fault that needs live diagnosis — and the cost of waiting is freeze-damaged product.

causes: Door open or gasket not sealing — the most common walk-in alarm is usually door- or defrost-related, not mechanical
Warm product loaded or heavy door traffic — recovery takes time
A defrost that just finished
A dust-blocked condenser coil, dead condenser fan, or tripped breaker
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||HI.fixable: Often, yes. Door, gasket, loading, post-defrost recovery, condenser airflow, and the breaker are all staff checks — give the box a couple of hours to recover with the door shut.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||HI.why_tech: If temperature keeps rising or won't recover in that window, the fault is in the sealed system — gauge diagnosis requiring EPA Section 608 certification, with product warming the whole time.

causes: The controller detected an error in its stored unit parameters — internal memory
Configuration data possibly corrupted
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||EE.fixable: Power-cycle once, press SET for a second to confirm the setpoint still reads what it should, and monitor the box with an independent thermometer. No parameter tinkering.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||EE.why_tech: A persistent memory error means the program has to be reloaded or the controller replaced by a tech — until then the box may be running on corrupted settings.

causes: An error in the stored operating parameters — working settings and setpoints
Settings may have reverted or corrupted
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||EF.fixable: Power-cycle once, compare the setpoint against what's posted for the unit, and watch box temperature independently. If EF returns or settings look wrong, stop there.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||EF.why_tech: The parameter set needs reloading from records by someone who has them — running on reverted setpoints can quietly hold the box at the wrong temperature in either direction.

causes: The defrost hit its maximum duration (dP) before reaching the end-defrost temperature (dt) — more ice on the coil than the defrost can clear
Humid-air leaks at the door gasket icing the coil between defrosts
Ice or overflow in the drain pan
A weak defrost heater, bad probe, or undersized defrost schedule
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||Ed.fixable: The diagnosis help is: look at the coil right after a defrost — remaining ice confirms it — check the door gasket, eyeball the drain pan, and note whether Ed shows after every defrost.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||Ed.why_tech: A repeating Ed means the defrost heater, probe, or schedule needs service — heater testing is live electrical work — and an uncorrected coil eventually blocks solid and stops the box cooling.

causes: A defrost is in progress and the display flashes dF (when parameter d6 = 0) — normal operation, not an error
During defrost the fans may be off and the box may warm slightly — also normal
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||dF.fixable: Yes — wait it out and avoid opening the door during defrost. Only if dF never clears well beyond the normal defrost time should it be treated as a fault.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||dF.why_tech: A unit that appears stuck in defrost, or won't pull back down afterward, has a defrost termination or control fault — probe and heater diagnosis is a live-electrical service job.

causes: Condenser temperature past the pre-alarm level — an early warning the coil is dirty or starved of airflow
Dust, lint, or grease blocking the fins so the coil can't reject heat
Items stored against or on top of the condensing unit
A condenser fan not running with the compressor
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||cht.fixable: Yes — this warning exists so staff can act before it escalates. Clear the airflow, check the fan, and get the dirt off the coil while it's still a pre-alarm.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||cht.why_tech: If it keeps returning after the airflow is cleared, the coil needs a professional cleaning — a condenser running hot is quietly loading the compressor every hour it runs.

causes: Condenser temperature over the Ac alarm threshold — the escalated version of cht, with buzzer and alarm relay active
A stopped condenser fan
A heavily matted coil or blocked airflow that the pre-alarm stage didn't get fixed
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||CHt.fixable: Check the fan and clear visible blockages, but don't keep silencing the alarm to force operation — that's how a dirty-coil warning turns into a dead compressor.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||CHt.why_tech: Continued running against a hard high-condenser alarm risks safety trips and compressor damage — a tech needs to clean the coil properly and verify the unit before it's trusted again.

causes: On PJEZ models with a real-time clock, the clock failed or lost its setting — often after a power outage
Time-of-day defrost bands won't run correctly until it's reset
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||EtC.fixable: Sometimes. After an outage, a trained operator re-setting the clock parameters may resolve it. Verify scheduled defrosts still occur at their normal times.
PJ Easy (PJEZ)||EtC.why_tech: A clock that won't hold time points to failed hardware — the controller may need replacement, and until then the defrost schedule the box depends on isn't running when it should.
